food.text: Byzantine cuisine grew out of local ancient Greek, ancient Roman and wider Mediterranean cooking. Trade with foreigners brought in grains, sugar, livestock, fruits, vegetables and spices that would otherwise have been limited to particular climates.

Byzantine citizens slaughtered pigs at the beginning of winter. This gave their families sausages, salt pork and lard to last the whole year. Pork was the single most common preserved meat, and pig bones made up nearly half of all animal remains at the site of Gritille in eastern Turkey.

Bread played a major part in the Byzantine diet, and the most valued kind was made from finely sieved wheat flour with no other grains mixed in. Bread was also made using rye, millet, egg yolks and chickpeas. Bulgur was eaten too.
Several familiar Greek foods are traced back to Byzantium: feta cheese, avgotaraho (cured fish roe), moustalevria and paximadi. Paximadi is a traditional hard bread baked from wheat, barley and rye.

Byzantine cooks experimented with new combinations of food and ended up with two styles. One was an eastern style, found in Asia Minor and the eastern Aegean, that added trade items to Byzantine cooking. The other was a leaner style based mainly on local Greek food culture.

Hunting deer and wild boar was a favourite and distinguished occupation for Byzantine men. They usually hunted with dogs and hawks, though they sometimes used trapping, netting and bird-liming, which means catching birds on sticky lime. Larger animals were a more expensive and rare food.

Historians disagree about what the average Byzantine ate. Some, including John L. Teall, Alexander Kazhdan and Giles Constable, suggested people were undernourished on bread, vegetables and wine. Joanita Vroom argued that grains, pulses, fruit, dairy, fish, meat, wine, olive oil and honey were all part of the typical diet.
Some ancient and Byzantine foods are no longer eaten in Greece. These include porridge (hilós), which was once the main staple, garos fish sauce, and salt water mixed into wine.
Only upper middle and higher Byzantines could afford lamb. Beef was seldom eaten because cattle were needed to cultivate the fields.

Fresh meat was mostly eaten by wealthy Byzantines, while poorer citizens ate more salted meat. Dried and salted meat was also one of the basic rations served to Byzantine soldiers. Poorer households also boiled the heads and feet of animals, and innards were boiled or fried.
Millet was cooked into gruel and porridge such as trachanas in Byzantine kitchens. Rye, millet, oats and vetch were mainly grown as animal fodder and were not preferred for human consumption.

art.text: Byzantine art emerged from Late Antiquity in about 500 CE. It soon formed a tradition distinct from that of Catholic Europe, though it had great influence over it. It was the art of the Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire.

During the Byzantine iconoclasm of 730 to 843, the vast majority of icons, sacred images usually painted on wood, were destroyed. So little remains that any new discovery sheds new understanding of the art.

Byzantine art was extremely conservative for religious and cultural reasons, yet it kept a continuous tradition of Greek realism. That realism contended with a strong anti-realist and hieratic impulse.
In the early medieval period the best Byzantine art often came from the large Imperial workshops. It represented an ideal of sophistication and technique that European patrons tried to emulate.

The term Byzantine art can also cover states that were contemporary with the Byzantine Empire and shared a common culture with it without being part of it. Bulgaria, Russia and Venice are named as examples.
Because so few icons survived iconoclasm, most remaining early works are in Italy, in Rome and Ravenna, or in Egypt at Saint Catherine's Monastery.

Icon production resumed in 843 after iconoclasm ended. From then until 1453 the Byzantine art tradition continued with relatively few changes, despite, or perhaps because of, the slow decline of the Empire.

Court art of the 10th century saw a notable revival of classical style, seen in works like the Paris Psalter. It shows how Byzantine artists could look back to older models even within a conservative tradition.

Famous examples of Balkan–Danubian architecture are the early Bulgarian capitals of Pliska and Preslav, as well as the Palace of Omurtag and the Murfatlar Cave Complex. Byzantine influence was stronger in the south, so finds in the north are entirely Slavic with some Turkic impression.

Byzantine manuscript illumination shows parallel styles, often used by the same artist. Iconic figures appear in framed miniatures, while informal small scenes or figures are added unframed in the margins in a much more realist style.

war.text: In 926 the armies of the Bulgarian Empire under Tsar Simeon I fought the Kingdom of Croatia under Tomislav in the Dinaric Alps of Eastern Bosnia, near the rivers Bosna and Drina. The result was an overwhelming Croatian victory.

Simeon I of Bulgaria aimed to defeat the Byzantine Empire and conquer Constantinople. To achieve this he overran the eastern and central Balkans several times, occupied Serbia and finally attacked Croatia.

At the start of the Early Middle Ages, Slavic tribes began to expand aggressively into Central and Southeastern Europe, including former Byzantine possessions in the Balkans. The Slavs and the Avars devastated the region, and large areas of the Balkans became depopulated. Bulgar and Slavic tribes also invaded Illyria, Thrace and even Greece.

In 924 Simeon sent a large army against Zaharija in the Principality of Serbia. The Bulgarian armies ravaged Serbia and forced Zaharija to flee to Croatia, and Simeon annexed Serbia. Tomislav then received and protected the Serbs whom Simeon had expelled from Rascia, and the Bulgarian state now bordered Tomislav's Croatia.

In 839 Presian I of Bulgaria invaded Serbia, starting a three-year war. Prince Vlastimir's army expelled Presian, who lost a large number of men and made no territorial gains. The Serbs had an advantage in the forests and gorges.

In 853 or 854 a Bulgarian army led by Vladimir-Rasate, son of Boris I, invaded Serbia. The Serbian army, led by Mutimir and his two brothers, defeated the Bulgars and captured Vladimir and 12 boyars. Peace was then agreed, and the prisoners were released.

The Croatian forces completely destroyed the Bulgarians in 926. Arguably key to the overwhelming victory was the choice of terrain: the Bulgarians were in an unfavorable position when the battle started, and the Croatian army attacked them by surprise. Duke Alogobotur, the Bulgarian commander, most likely perished in the battle along with most of his soldiers, since he is no longer mentioned in sources.

Serbia became a key part of the power struggle between the Byzantines and Bulgarians, mostly allied with the Byzantines. In 924 Simeon I sent a large army that forced Zaharija to flee, then summoned the Serbian župans to recognize Časlav as prince. When they came, they were all imprisoned and taken to Bulgaria, as Časlav was too. Much of Serbia was ravaged and many people fled to Croatia, Bulgaria and Constantinople, and Simeon annexed the principality. In 933 Časlav was established as ruler and became the most powerful ruler of the Vlastimirović dynasty.

The Balkans was politically decentralized and unstable for a long time, and in the Early Middle Ages was known as the Sclaveni or Slav lands. War captives were sold by their enemies to Venetian slave traders at the coasts, turning people taken in war into enslaved people shipped abroad. The trade lasted from the 7th century until the mid-15th century. Most of those trafficked went to the Islamic Middle East, with the majority of the slaves sent to Egypt (around 2,000 a year) being boys, bought to serve as Mamluk slave soldiers, while most of those sold in Italy and Spain were girls, intended to become ancillae, enslaved domestic servants.

According to Constantine VII, Serbs and Bulgars lived peacefully as neighbours until the Bulgar invasion of 839. It is not known exactly what prompted the war, as Porphyrogenitus gives no clear answer.

After the Serbian victory in 853, Mutimir's sons Pribislav and Stefan escorted the prisoners to the border. There Boris I gave them rich gifts, while he received two slaves, two falcons, two dogs and 80 furs.

Thirteen sites in the Danube Basin of Serbia (Vojvodina) show early Slavic presence, dated to the late 6th century or later. The article says these Slavs possibly served as foederati protecting Byzantine border fortresses.

literature.text: From the 7th century onwards, Greek was the only language of administration and government in the Byzantine Empire. Under Emperor Heraclius (610–641 AD), who took the Greek title Basileus in 610, Greek became the official language of the Eastern Roman Empire.

Unlike monasteries in Western Europe, religious houses in the Byzantine world rarely maintained their own copying centres. Instead they acquired books through donations from wealthy donors, and travelling monks were often given funds to buy books.

Medieval Greek writers made concessions to the spoken language. John Malalas's Chronography from the 6th century, the Chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor (9th century) and the works of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (mid-10th century) were influenced by the vernacular in word choice and idiom, though they largely followed written Koine.

Greek in the Byzantine Empire is listed among the classical languages inherited from earlier epochs that remained in active literary use during the 6th through 9th centuries. It stood alongside Latin, Chinese, Sanskrit, Persian and Hebrew.

From the beginning of the 6th century, amendments to the law in the Eastern Roman Empire were mostly written in Greek. Parts of the Roman Corpus Iuris Civilis were also gradually translated into Greek.

In Constantinople, Latin at first remained the language of both the court and the army, and was used for official documents. Its influence waned, but Latin continued to appear on the coinage and in certain court ceremonies up to the 11th century.

science.text: In the early centuries of the Middle Ages, from 400 to 1000 CE, knowledge of Greek ideas about the world deteriorated in Latin-speaking Western Europe. In the Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire, that knowledge continued to thrive.

At the beginning of the Middle Ages, the Byzantine Empire was the leading center of scientific scholarship in its region. It supplied the medieval Islamic world with Ancient and early Medieval Greek texts on astronomy, mathematics and philosophy, which were then translated into Arabic.
science.source_title: Greek contributions to the Islamic world

science.text: The Antikythera mechanism, a 37-gear device from 150 to 100 BC, calculated the motions of the Sun and Moon. It may have belonged to a Greek tradition of complex mechanical technology that was later, at least in part, passed on to the Byzantine and Islamic worlds. There, complex but simpler mechanical devices were built during the Middle Ages.

In the sixth century, Isidore of Miletus compiled Archimedes' mathematical works in the Archimedes Palimpsest. This gathered all of Archimedes' mathematical contributions in one place, where they could be collected and studied within the Byzantine Empire.

Fragments of a geared calendar attached to a sundial have been found from the fifth or sixth century Byzantine Empire, and it may have been used to help tell time. Around 1000, the scientist al-Biruni described a similar geared calendar, showing that the idea lasted for centuries.

In the ninth century the Byzantine emperor sent Saint Cyril on an embassy to the Arabs. His Muslim hosts were astonished by his knowledge of philosophy and science as well as theology, a sign of how much learning Byzantine scholars carried.
science.source_title: Greek contributions to the Islamic world

politics.text: The Byzantine Empire reached its greatest extent under Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565. He briefly reconquered much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast. A plague that began around 541 was devastating: it killed a large proportion of the population and severely reduced the empire's social and financial stability. Long warfare with Persia added fiscal and military strain.

The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 680 to 681, when Bulgars led by Asparuh moved into the northeastern Balkans. They defeated the Byzantine army led by Constantine IV and won Byzantine recognition of their right to settle south of the Danube. By the 9th and 10th centuries Bulgaria could compete with the Byzantine Empire.

Under Emperor Heraclius, who also took the Greek title Basileus in 610, Greek became the official language of the Eastern Roman Empire. Its people still called themselves Rhomaioi, or Romans, because they saw their state as the continuation of Roman rule. Latin lingered on coinage and in some court ceremonies until the 11th century.

The first Serbian state with an established political identity was founded by prince Vlastimir in the mid-9th century. Serbs were then caught between Bulgarians, Hungarians and Byzantines, and between Rome and Constantinople over Christianization. The Byzantines got the upper hand in the 9th century.

Under Umar, the second Caliph, the Muslims decisively conquered Syria and Mesopotamia, as well as Roman Palestine, Roman Egypt, parts of Asia Minor and Roman North Africa, while entirely toppling the Sasanids. Heraclius's successors later salvaged Constantinople from two Arab sieges, in 674 to 677 and in 717. The 8th and early 9th century empire was then rocked by the Iconoclastic Controversy, punctuated by dynastic struggles between factions at court. The Bulgars and Slavs profited from the disorder and invaded Illyria, Thrace and even Greece; after their decisive victory at Ongala in 680 they defeated the Byzantines again and forced them to sign a humiliating peace treaty recognising the First Bulgarian Empire.

Bulgaria adopted Christianity in 864, an outcome of strong Byzantine cultural influence. The two powers were often hostile, and Bulgaria became Byzantium's primary threat to the north. Yet they also allied during the Second Arab Siege of Constantinople, where the Bulgarian army broke the siege and destroyed the Arab army. According to the article, the Bulgarians slaughtered between 22,000 and 30,000 Arabs in the decisive battle before the Walls of Constantinople, forcing them to abandon the undertaking.

In 839 Presian I launched an invasion of Serbian territory, which led to a war that lasted three years. Vlastimir, who had united the Serbian tribes, won it: the Bulgarian army was heavily defeated and lost a large number of its men, and Presian made no territorial gains and was driven out by the army of Vlastimir. The Serbs are believed to have held out in their defensible forests and gorges and to have known how to fight in the hills. Emperor Theophilos was recognized as the nominal overlord of the Serbs and most likely encouraged them to thwart the Bulgars.

Khan Krum issued the first known written Bulgarian law code at a People's Council at the start of the 9th century. Only parts survive, preserved in the 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia Suda. It prescribed the death penalty for false oaths and accusations, and severe penalties for thieves and those who sheltered them. Many historians see it as an attempt to centralise the state under a single code of laws.

In 924 Simeon I sent a large army, accompanied by Časlav, against Serbia, and annexed the Principality of Serbia. The Serbian župans were summoned to recognize Časlav as prince, but when they came they were all imprisoned and taken to Bulgaria, as Časlav was too. Much of Serbia was ravaged and many people fled to Croatia, Bulgaria and Constantinople. Bulgarian rule lasted until 933, when Časlav led the refugees back and became the most powerful ruler of the Vlastimirović dynasty; around 969 to 971 the Byzantine Empire annexed the principality and ruled it as the Catepanate of Ras.

After Byzantine Emperor Nicephorus I captured Pliska in 811, he found large quantities of wine there. This contradicts the Suda's claim that Krum's laws ordered all vineyards uprooted. Contemporary sources also say that after the final Bulgarian victory, Krum drank wine in the Emperor's skull. The article says Nicephorus I was slain along with most of his troops at the Varbitsa Pass, and that his skull was lined with silver and used as a drinking cup.

The Royal Frankish Annals mention the Serbs in 822 as holding a great part of Dalmatia. The unnamed 7th-century ancestor of the Serbian dynasty reportedly fled to Emperor Heraclius. Porphyrogenitos gives the family line as Višeslav, Radoslav, Prosigoj and Vlastimir.

philosophy.text: In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea met to restore the use and veneration of icons, which had been suppressed by imperial edict in the Byzantine Empire. It is recognized as the last of the first seven ecumenical councils by the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches.

The Byzantine Iconoclasm refers to two periods when religious images were opposed by religious and imperial authorities, leading to several civil wars. The First Iconoclasm ran from about 726 to 787, and the Second from 814 to 842. It was accompanied by widespread destruction of religious images and persecution of those who venerated them. According to the surviving iconophile sources, Constantine V burned monasteries and images, had relics thrown into the sea, and forced monks to parade in the Hippodrome hand-in-hand with women in violation of their vows; in 765 St Stephen the Younger was killed and later considered a martyr.

Bogomilism was a Christian dualist sect founded in the First Bulgarian Empire by the priest Bogomil during the reign of Tsar Peter I in the 10th century. It most likely arose in the region of Kutmichevitsa, today part of Macedonia.

Cyril and Methodius, Byzantine brothers, are credited with devising the Glagolitic alphabet, the first alphabet used to transcribe Old Church Slavonic. Known as the "Apostles to the Slavs", they helped spread Christianity throughout Eastern Europe through their work and that of their disciples.

The Second Council of Nicaea ruled that honorary veneration of icons was permitted, while true adoration was reserved for God alone. It stated that honor given to an icon passes through to its subject, so it is not idolatrous as the iconoclasts believed. The Incarnation of Christ was emphasized as making his depiction acceptable.

Theodore the Studite, abbot of the Stoudios Monastery in Constantinople, was a zealous opponent of iconoclasm. His reforms emphasized communal life, manual labor and a carefully defined administrative hierarchy. Elements of his Testament were later incorporated into the typika of early Athonite monasteries.

Photios I served as Patriarch of Constantinople from 858 to 867 and from 877 to 886. He is regarded as the most important intellectual of his time, called "the leading light of the ninth-century renaissance". His famous library reflected learning in theology, philosophy, law and medicine.

Constantine V banned icon veneration and supported the Council of Hieria in 754, which called itself the seventh ecumenical council. His vigorous enforcement of the ban included persecution of those who venerated icons and of monks in general. Images of emperors were still allowed, which some opponents saw as giving wider authority to imperial power than to the saints and bishops. The Second Council of Nicaea overturned the Council of Hieria only 33 years later.
After Leo IV's early death, his widow Irene of Athens, as regent for her son, began the restoration of icons. She acted out of personal inclination and political considerations.
Photios I wrote two "mirrors of princes", one addressed to Boris-Michael of Bulgaria and the other to Leo VI the Wise. He was also a central figure in the conversion of the Slavs to Christianity.

Boris I, wary of Byzantine influence, established literary schools in Pliska and Ohrid where theology was taught in Slavonic. Clement of Ohrid taught some 3,500 students over seven years, from 886 to 893, in the Slavonic language and the Glagolitic alphabet.

Some accounts credit Theodore the Studite with the first recorded stand against slavery itself, in the ninth century. He is quoted as commanding "Thou shalt possess no slave", because man is made in the image of God.

culture.text: From the 7th century onwards, Greek was the only language of administration and government in the Byzantine Empire. This stage of the language is therefore called Byzantine Greek, and it links the older Koine Greek to Modern Greek.

In the tenth century, the largest book collection in the Byzantine world was found in the monasteries of Mount Athos. It had accumulated over 10,000 books. Scholars travelled from monastery to monastery in search of the texts they wished to study.

Slavs began mass migrating into Southeastern Europe between the first half of the 6th and the 7th century. Greece was settled only from the 7th century, although military invasions could be argued from the mid-6th century. The Plague of Justinian had decimated the native population, and the Slavs settled lands that were often devastated: Roman fortifications were destroyed and the native population was often decimated, with Slavs settling in the ruined lands and often replacing the people who had lived there.

Because Medieval Greek was the language of the Eastern Orthodox Church, it entered the Slavic languages through religion after Cyril and Methodius converted the Slavs. It passed into Old Church Slavonic and later into Bulgarian, Russian, Ukrainian, Serbian and Romanian.

The Slavs reached Serbian lands with distinctive material culture, and archaeologists have found fibulae and Slavic pottery at Roman forts. Finds suggest that a good part of the native Roman population stayed and lived within and near the old ramparts.

The Christianization of Bulgaria was made official in 864, during the reign of Knyaz Boris I. It came amid shifting political alliances with the Byzantine Empire, the kingdom of the East Franks and the Pope. The most significant missionary work among the Slavs took place in the mid-ninth century.

The Balkan–Danubian culture emerged in the Lower Danube region in the 8th century and flourished until the 11th century. Known as Pliska–Preslav culture in Bulgaria, it combined Slavic and Bulgar elements. Its famous examples include the early Bulgarian capitals of Pliska and Preslav and the Palace of Omurtag.

The Balkan–Danubian culture flourished in the Lower Danube region from the 8th century until the 11th century. It is called the Pliska–Preslav culture in Bulgaria and the Dridu culture in Romania. It combined Slavic and Bulgar elements, with some Romance components in the south.

Written Greek largely followed the models of written Koine, but some authors let the spoken language slip in. Concessions to the vernacular appear in John Malalas's 6th-century Chronography, the 9th-century Chronicle of Theophanes the Confessor, and the works of Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus in the mid-10th century.

Byzantine religious houses rarely ran their own copying centres, unlike many monasteries in Western Europe. Instead they acquired books through donations from wealthy donors. Travelling monks were often given funds to buy books.

Early Slavic settlements in Serbia were unfortified and small, and no cemetery has been found. Burial was mainly cremation and later biritual. After Christianization from the mid-9th century, settlements grew in number and became fortified.
